newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Sepracor eyes albuterol coup.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Sepracor eyes albuterol coup.

text.p: Sepracor Inc said it will file a new drug application on Tuesday with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its "purified" nebuliser form of albuterol, with hopes of dominating that $250 million segment of the market for the bronchodilator asthma drug.

Sepracor also aims to seize the lion's share of the worldwide $1.5 billion albuterol market within five years by developing oral forms of its purified drug, levalbuterol, Chief Financial Officer David Southwell told Reuters.

Pending an expected year-long FDA review, Southwell said Sepracor is building a 50-person sales team to market levalbuterol to hospitals. They use mask-like nebulisers to deliver fine-mist dosages of drugs.
"We are building a hospital-based sales force to be in a position to sell it ourselves," Southwell said, adding the company had the means with about $120 million in cash on hand.

"We think we can potentially dominate the whole albuterol market. We could easily get more than half," said Southwell, whose company purifies existing drugs to make new patentable forms lacking the side effects of original drugs.
Most conventional drug molecules have two mirror images, or isomers. One typically provides the desired effect while the other "evil twin" often brings unwanted side effects.
Sepracor, with expertise in removing unwanted isomers, has won product patents in the past five years on single-isomer forms of 20 marketed drugs, including albuterol.
Its drugs can only be sold once patents expire on original drugs, or by licensing agreement with original drug makers in cases where patents are still in force.
Sepracor said it aims to leapfrog over Glaxo Wellcome and Schering-Plough Corp, whose respective off-patent prescription drugs Ventolin and Proventil now dominate the albuterol market.
Timothy Barberich, Sepracor chief executive officer, said the company will press ahead with broader clinical trials of levalbuterol to reinforce results of its completed Phase III nebuliser trials.
"If we can underscore the results in greater numbers of patients, it really makes the prospect of 100 percent market penetration a real possibility," Barberich said.

Over the next 18 months, the company said it plans to submit separate new drug applications for levalbuterol in syrup formulation, controlled-release tablets, a metered-dose inhaler and a dry powder inhaler.
In Phase III adult trials, patients receiving a nebuliser dose of levalbuterol showed similar relief as patients receiving four-times-larger doses of standard unpurified forms of albuterol.
Levalbuterol showed fewer side effects such as the increased pulse rate, tremor, nervousness and changes in glucose blood levels linked to standard forms of albuterol.
"The data looks quite good. It looks like Sepracor will have levalbuterol on the market late next year," said David Steinberg, a pharmaceuticals analyst with Volpe, Brown, Whelan & Co.
"It could create a nice niche for itself because it appears to have a favourable side-effect profile. It could be looked at as a medically superior product," he added.
"And the FDA seems to clearly be on the side of single-isomer products," Steinberg added, noting the agency in 1992 began stating its preference of them over "racemic," or twin-isomer forms.
Sepracor's first product, Allegra, is a single-isomer version of Hoechst AG's blockbuster antihistamine Seldane.

Hoechst unit Hoechst Marion Roussel licensed Allegra from Sepracor in 1993 and agreed to pay the startup a single-digit royalty fee on U.S. sales when Seldane's composition-of-matter patent expires in 1999.
But the FDA pulled Seldane off the market earlier this year soon after Hoechst began marketing Allegra, citing Seldane's potentially severe cardiac side effects.
In effect, Allegra -- freed in the chemist's lab from its "evil twin" -- was also freed from having to compete in the marketplace with its less-safe parent drug.
